books.section: Great Depression and the New Deal (1929-1939)

primary_sources: Federal Reserve Bulletin, September 1937, Table 1 (bank suspensions, 1921-1936)

stimulus.text:
| Year | Banks that closed |
| 1929 | 659 |
| 1930 | 1,350 |
| 1931 | 2,293 |
| 1932 | 1,453 |
| 1933 | 4,000 |

Bank suspensions in the United States, 1929–1933. The 1933 figure counts banks closed in the banking crisis and not licensed to reopen after the March 1933 bank holiday.
stimulus.source_note: Figures from the Federal Reserve Bulletin, September 1937, Table 1 (bank suspensions, 1921–1936).

source: original; stimulus table built from Federal Reserve Bulletin, September 1937, Table 1
stem: The bank-failure table best supports which of the following conclusions?

options.text: Bank failures were rare until the New Deal began
options.misconception: The table shows hundreds of banks closing every year from 1929 on, years before the New Deal began in 1933.

options.text: The crash ended bank failures after 1931
options.misconception: Failures kept coming after 1931: 1,453 in 1932 and 4,000 in 1933.

options.text: Bank failures were common before the crash, then surged
Most banks that closed in 1933 soon reopened
options.misconception: The table counts banks that closed. The 1933 figure includes banks never licensed to reopen after the bank holiday.

rationales.A: Background from the books: rural banks had already been closing at a high rate during the 1920s, and 659 closed in 1929 itself.
rationales.B: The table itself refutes this: 1,453 banks closed in 1932 and 4,000 in 1933, after 1931.
rationales.C: Background from the books: 659 banks closed in 1929 and rural banks had failed through the 1920s; then the count more than doubled in 1930 and peaked at 4,000 in 1933.
rationales.D: Background from the books: the 1933 figure counts banks closed in the crisis and not licensed to reopen after the March 1933 bank holiday.
rationales.general:
1. Read the first row: 659 banks closed in 1929, the crash year.
2. Read the trend: the count more than doubles in 1930 and peaks in 1933.
3. Ask what that pattern means. Background from the books: failures were already common in the 1920s, then surged.
4. The table shows failures common before the crash, then surging.
Remember: read a table row by row before judging it, since the first row sets the baseline.
